system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker MUT_SMARCA4 (damaging SMARCA4 mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

input.mechanism:
SMARCA2 and SMARCA4 are mutually exclusive paralogous ATPases of the SWI/SNF (BAF) complex. Loss of SMARCA4 leaves SMARCA2-containing BAF complexes as the only ATPase-competent form, making them essential for chromatin accessibility and lineage gene expression. Selective SMARCA2 knockdown should therefore kill SMARCA4-mutant cells while sparing SMARCA4-wild-type cells, which can use SMARCA4.</mechanism>
<parameter name="novelty">well_established

findings.claim: SMARCA4 damaging-mutant cancer lines are selectively dependent on the paralog SMARCA2 (SWI/SNF ATPase synthetic lethality). Discovery: t=-10.26, q=1.3e-18, 14/35 altered lines strongly dependent vs 11/591 others, robust across lineages (Lung, Biliary, Pleura, CNS). Held-out Broad lines replicated strongly (23 altered, t=-6.9, one-sided p=1.1e-11). Independent Sanger screen failed (only 6 altered lines, beta positive, p=0.90), so it did not pass the pre-registered criterion.

input.summary: Best candidate: SMARCA2, the paralog of SMARCA4. Across 626 discovery lines, MUT_SMARCA4 is the strongest selective dependency signal in the data (the next-best hits are weak and non-significant). The association holds after lineage adjustment and is not driven by a single lineage: 14/35 altered lines are strongly dependent on SMARCA2, versus 11/591 others. SMARCA2 is not broadly essential. The held-out Broad lines confirmed it (p=1e-11). However, the independent Sanger screen did not replicate: it contained only 6 altered lines and showed no effect, so under the pre-registered criterion (p<0.01 in both) H1 is not replicated. The Sanger result is likely underpowered and may also reflect differences in mutation calling or library, so I treat the biology as credible but unconfirmed across labs. The mechanism is well established in the literature (SMARCA2 as the synthetic-lethal partner of SMARCA4 loss), so this is a validation of a known dependency rather than a novel finding. Other candidates (PRDX1, DYNLL1, ATMIN) were weaker, non-significant, or broadly essential, and were not registered.
